hints: Focus on how many electron shells are left after the electrons are lost, since fewer shells means a much smaller ion.
Notice that $\text{Na}^{+}$, $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ and $\text{Al}^{3+}$ all end up with the same 10-electron neon arrangement, but with 11, 12 and 13 protons pulling on them.
Compare the pull of the nucleus for those three isoelectronic ions, then check why the Period 6 ion must be far larger.
walkthrough:
**Separate by number of shells**

Think like a teacher: cations lose their outer shell, so count what is left. $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ still has electrons in 5 shells (xenon configuration), while the other three all drop to just 2 shells.

$$\text{Ba}^{2+} : [\text{Xe}] \text{ configuration, n = 5 left}$$

**Spot the isoelectronic set**

$\text{Na}^{+}$, $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ and $\text{Al}^{3+}$ all have 10 electrons, so they are isoelectronic with neon.

$$\text{Na}^{+} = 2,8 \quad \text{Mg}^{2+} = 2,8 \quad \text{Al}^{3+} = 2,8$$

**Use nuclear charge to rank them**

With the same number of electrons and shells, more protons means stronger pull and smaller radius. Nuclear charges are Na = 11, Mg = 12, Al = 13.

$$\text{radius decreases as proton number increases: } \text{Na}^{+} > \text{Mg}^{2+} > \text{Al}^{3+}$$

**Conclude the smallest**

$\text{Al}^{3+}$ has the highest charge density with 13 protons pulling only 10 electrons in just two shells, so it is smaller than $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ and $\text{Na}^{+}$, and far smaller than large $\text{Ba}^{2+}$.

options.A: Correct. $\text{Al}^{3+}$ has only the n=1 and n=2 shells (10 electrons) pulled in by 13 protons. That gives the greatest effective nuclear charge in the isoelectronic trio, so it is the smallest ion here.
options.B: Incorrect. $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ is in Period 6 and keeps many more filled shells than the others. More shells outweighs higher charge, so it is actually the largest ion, a common trap if you only look at the 2+ charge.
options.C: Incorrect. $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ is small because it is 2,8 with 12 protons, but $\text{Al}^{3+}$ has one more proton for the same electron arrangement. Students who stop at high charge without comparing proton numbers often pick this.
options.D: Incorrect. $\text{Na}^{+}$ is isoelectronic with the other two (2,8) but has only 11 protons. Less nuclear pull means its electrons are held less tightly, so it is larger than both $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ and $\text{Al}^{3+}$.
